title: Breath in the rule
hookLine: your breath practice: Barlaam mocked the praying monks' breathing, and Gregory Palamas answered him
tomorrow: a bush burned and didn't burn up. what did the voice ask of Moses?

lines: A SLOW EXHALE AT A RED LIGHT.
cards: Breathing apps, box breathing before a big meeting, a slow exhale at a red light. Some people swear by it; some roll their eyes. The eye-rolling is old.
A scholar named Barlaam, from Calabria in Italy, heard how some Greek monks prayed: chin down, eyes toward the chest, breath slowed on purpose, one short prayer said over and over. He laughed.
He called them navel-souls, as if they thought the soul lived in the belly button. A monk of Mount Athos decided that deserved an answer.

teach.h: BARLAAM: PRAYER IS THE MIND'S WORK.

teach.b: Prayer is the work of the mind, he said. Bending over, slowing your breath: that's mechanics, not prayer. The monk was Gregory Palamas, and he wrote the other side down.
The mind keeps wandering outward, he said. For beginners especially, slowing the breath helps gather it back inside, into the heart, where prayer happens. And the body isn't the enemy of prayer.

teach.h: THE JESUS PRAYER, WITH THE BREATH.
teach.b: The monks paired the breath with a short prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me. Again and again, with the breath, until it prays almost by itself.

This is hesychasm, from the Greek for stillness, and the Orthodox Church sided with Palamas; he's honored as a saint. But Barlaam's worry is worth hearing, not just losing. A method can become the point.

teach.h: A HELP FOR BEGINNERS, NOT THE GOAL.
teach.b: A calm body isn't the same thing as meeting God, and Palamas himself treated the breathing as a help for beginners, not the goal.
So the debate leaves you a good question. Breath alone is a technique. Breath carrying your attention toward something larger becomes a practice.
For your rule, that's the line to write: what will your breath carry?

how: In Orthodox Christian hesychasm, monks and lay people say the Jesus Prayer, sometimes paired with slow breathing. Breath practices also appear in Buddhist, Hindu and secular meditation; a personal rule names one.

games.q: what does “breath in the rule” mean?
o: a breathing app that tracks your heart rate during work
your written breath practice, with something for it to carry
holding your breath as long as you can to build strength

games.q: the breath debate: tap the pairs.
p: breath helps gather the mind inward
said again and again with the breath

s: Palamas taught that the breathing method was the goal of prayer
he treated it as a help for beginners, gathering the mind; the goal was prayer itself.
the Orthodox Church sided with Palamas and honors him as a saint
hesychasm, prayer with stillness and the breath, stayed part of Orthodox practice.
Barlaam's objection was that breathing slowly was unhealthy
his objection was that prayer is the mind's work, so body techniques weren't prayer.

games.q: you love your breath practice. a friend asks you to make the best case for Barlaam's side. what is it?
o: a method can become the point: a calm body isn't the same as meeting God.
breathing slowly while praying is bad for the body.
the monks were lazy and wanted an easy shortcut.
games.why: That's the strongest form of his worry, and Palamas partly agreed: the breathing was a help for beginners, not the goal.

practice: Sit with your chin slightly lowered, and slow your breath, in through the nose and out. If you pray, the Jesus Prayer can ride the breath, half on the in, half on the out.
If not, let each breath bring your attention home from wherever it wandered.

wordCard.voice: Breath in the rule: your breath practice, written in, with something for the breath to carry, as the monks of Athos taught.

orig.note: Greek: stillness, quiet. Hesychasm is Orthodox prayer of stillness.

carryVoice: Your line: breathe. Palamas let the breath gather the mind; Barlaam warned it isn't the goal. Day 1648, in and out.

sources.ref: Gregory Palamas, Triads in Defense of the Holy Hesychasts I.2 (on keeping the mind within the body; the breathing method as a help for beginners), written against Barlaam of Calabria
The Jesus Prayer ('Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me'), Orthodox tradition; cf. Luke 18:13
